description: We’re OddTerrain. A team that loves exploring new ideas, technology, and the world beyond our own. We’re building Planetary Analog Finder to discover places on Earth that look and feel like the Moon or Mars. We enjoy combining AI, data, research, and creativity to turn an interesting idea into something real.
summary:
We developed GeoX, an AI-powered app that finds places on Earth that match the conditions of the Moon and Mars. A user selects a target site, such as Jezero Crater, and GeoX reads its fingerprint from open NASA and ESA data: terrain, thermal behavior, aridity, vegetation, and bare ground. Our similarity model then scans Earth, ranks the closest analogues on a map and in a list, and gives each a 0-100 fidelity score with a side-by-side comparison. Reverse Mode lets anyone tap a globe to see how Mars-like or Moon-like their own location is, and Trends shows Earth becoming more Mars-like over time. Users can also suggest new candidate sites for review.

Today, analogue sites are chosen by hand, and the same few famous locations are reused again and again. GeoX answers the challenge with a fast, transparent search across the whole planet, so more candidate sites can be found and compared. This matters because better analogues make rover, spacesuit, and mission testing safer and cheaper before crews ever leave Earth. GeoX is also honest about its limits: no Earth site can reproduce gravity, radiation, or vacuum.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

GeoX finds places on Earth that are similar to sites on the Moon and Mars. Before astronauts or rovers go to another world, teams test equipment and train in similar places on Earth. Finding those places is slow, and teams often return to the same few famous sites, such as the Atacama Desert. GeoX searches the whole world with real data instead.

HOW IT WORKS

GeoX compares 600 Earth locations with 20 targets, 10 on Mars and 10 on the Moon, including Jezero Crater, Gale Crater and the lunar south pole.

For each Earth location we collect open satellite data through Google Earth Engine. Copernicus DEM gives slope and surface roughness. NASA MODIS gives surface temperature, the day to night temperature swing and vegetation (NDVI). ESA WorldCover gives bare ground. Target values come from physics-based formulas and published NASA and peer-reviewed sources.

Each site gets two scores. The environment score shows how close its measured values are to the target. The picture score uses DINOv2, a vision AI model, to compare a Sentinel-2 image of the site with the target image from NASA Solar System Treks. Earth images are first blurred to the target image's resolution so the comparison is fair. The final score is 75% environment and 25% picture.

KEY FEATURES

Reverse Mode. Pick a city instead of a planet and see how Moon- or Mars-like your own home is. Fourteen cities are scored.

Change over time. GeoX tracks 24 years of data (2001 to 2024) and asks whether a site is becoming more like its target. It uses Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test and reports a trend only when it is statistically significant. Only 3 of the 20 targets show one.

Honest about blind spots. Three lunar targets (Shackleton, Haworth and Cabeus) have flat, shadowed images. GeoX does not pretend to see them. It scores them on environment alone and tells the user why.

Ask GeoX. Users ask questions in plain words, such as "Which site is best for a rover?". Every answer comes only from stored results, so it never makes up a number.

Mission goals. Sites can be ranked for rover driving, geology, astrobiology, astronaut walks (EVA) or using local resources (ISRU).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

GeoX turns weeks of reading papers and comparing maps into minutes. It brings forward overlooked sites, which can mean cheaper and closer test locations, including for teams in countries far from the famous analogue sites. Reverse Mode and Ask GeoX also make planetary science easy for students and the public to explore. GeoX does not replace field testing or expert judgement. It helps teams take the first step faster.

DOES IT WORK?

We tested GeoX against 11 known analogue sites used in real research and 10 control sites chosen before any scoring. For all 19 targets the test applies to, the known analogues scored significantly higher than the controls. We also report a weakness openly. On this test, the environment score alone separates the groups more clearly than the combined score. We fixed the 75/25 weight before testing and did not change it to improve the result.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Languages: Python and Dart.

Data and AI: Google Earth Engine, Kaggle GPU notebooks, PyTorch (DINOv2), scikit-learn, SciPy, NumPy and pandas.

App: Flutter for the app, FastAPI for the backend that scores new points picked on the map, and Supabase for sign-in.

Hardware: no special hardware. Our team used personal laptops and free cloud GPUs.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Most analogue searches look only at maps or only at images. GeoX combines measured environment data with AI image similarity. Reverse Mode flips the usual question. The trend feature asks whether places on Earth are slowly becoming more Mars-like. Honesty is built into the design: GeoX shows when data is missing and never invents answers.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Fair comparison: Earth images are matched to each target image's resolution, and elevation and dryness are left out because they are measured differently on other worlds.

Honest results: the controls were chosen before scoring, and the weights were fixed in advance.

Limits: GeoX cannot reproduce gravity, air pressure or radiation, and says so.

Access: the main results are stored inside the app, so most features work without a server or internet.\
